sections.html:
Three routes get a Scranton house sold: a cash offer, an agent listing, or doing it yourself. Cash has the fewest moving parts. Scranton sits in Lackawanna County, and the city has its own rules for permits, rental licenses and transfer tax that can slow a conventional sale.

A listing leans on a buyer's lender, an appraisal and a repair list. Cash skips nearly all of it, which suits the house is inherited, has tenants, needs work, or sits on a street where older homes take longer to move. The cost is price. Cash offers usually come in under a polished listing, so get both numbers first.

Homes sit on hills between roughly 650 and 1,400 feet above sea level, which puts lot slope, drainage and retaining walls on many inspection reports. Most older housing dates from the anthracite and railroad years: narrow lots, brick and frame doubles, steep driveways and basements that have seen decades of freeze and thaw. Green Ridge and the mountain neighborhoods read very differently to a buyer than the older streets near downtown, so a price from one area says little about another.

Sellers in Scranton face a combined realty transfer tax of 3.7 percent of the value, against 2 percent across most of Lackawanna County. No deed gets recorded until the tax is paid.

The state's piece is 1 percent, and the rest goes to local government and the school district. The county Recorder collects it all. Your sales agreement settles who pays, often a split, though the new owner is on the hook if the amount is ever questioned.

  • Transfers within a family, parent to child or between siblings, are exempt. Non-profit corporations get no such exemption.
  • A deed showing token consideration of $1 must carry a Statement of Value for state review.

City rules say each rental property needs a rental license. Renting an unlicensed unit is a violation. Renew by March 15 every year. A newly rented unit needs its license within 30 days of a tenant moving in.

The fee scales with unit count: $45 per unit at one to three units, rising to a $450 flat fee at fifty or more. A unit lived in by family still needs a license but costs nothing. The city inspects every three years, and the first re-inspection carries no charge.

Selling with tenants still in the unit? Bring the license up to date first. Lenders and investors both ask to see it, and a lapse can mean a refused license or fines. The rental licensing office can tell you where your property stands, so call before you choose a closing day.

sections.h2: Vacant, in default or heading to a tax sale
sections.html:
Registration with the city is required for any property, occupied or empty, in any of these situations: mortgage default, a lis pendens, a foreclosure action, a tax deed application, a pending tax lien sale, or a deed in lieu to the lender. There is no fee, and you register on the city's online portal.

The abandoned label stays until the house sells, the foreclosure is dismissed or the default is cured. A sale that closes before a judgment or tax sale ends the status, which is where a quick cash closing can help. Call the Lackawanna County Tax Claim Bureau for the exact upset sale dates that apply to your parcel.

sections.h2: Permits and repairs before you sell
sections.html:
A seller in Pennsylvania has no duty to renovate. If you do start work in Scranton, get a permit first, because every construction project needs one before work begins. The city exempts only painting and gutter installation.

Plans follow the 2021 International Code Council series, and existing buildings fall under the 2024 International Property Maintenance Code. Three more checks can catch a seller off guard:

  • A home in a historic district or landmark needs a Certificate of Appropriateness for exterior changes, building permit or not.
  • Work in a FEMA flood zone goes through the floodplain administrator. Improvements worth 50 percent or more of market value require elevation or flood-proofing.
  • Fences, sheds and pools can need zoning approval even without a building permit.

Code Enforcement's in-person counter is at 338 N Washington Avenue. Title companies often hold up a closing over open or expired permits. Request the permit history from the office before you list.

Underground anthracite workings lie beneath much of Scranton, and ordinary homeowner policies usually leave out damage from collapsed mines. The Department of Environmental Protection runs a Mine Subsidence Insurance program to cover that.

Policies range from $5,000 to $1,000,000, and $150,000 of residential coverage costs $41.25 a year. A risk map from DEP shows whether an address sits over mined ground, and a buyer's lender may ask. A policy does not transfer to the new owner, who has to apply for their own, and a seller who cancels at closing can get unused premium back when the notice arrives inside a month of the sale.

Cracks can also come from soil settlement or frost, so have an inspector look before you assume the worst.

sections.h2: Winter and the condition of the house
sections.html: An average Scranton year brings 45.1 inches of snow and about 39 days when the high stays below freezing. That freeze-thaw cycle is hard on roofs, gutters, chimneys, retaining walls, concrete steps and old foundations, and buyers' inspectors look for exactly those items. A buyer who purchases as-is removes the need to schedule repairs around the weather.

sections.h2: Steps for a quick Scranton sale
sections.html:
1. Pull the deed and any mortgage or lien payoff figures.
  2. If anyone rents the property, confirm the rental license is current before you list.
  3. Ask Code Enforcement for the permit history, and close out open or expired permits.
  4. If the house is in default or facing a tax sale, register it through the city's online portal and call the Tax Claim Bureau about upset sale dates.
  5. Decide in the sales agreement who pays the 3.7 percent transfer tax.
  6. Have the closing agent record the deed with the Recorder of Deeds, which will not take it until the tax is paid.

A cash sale can close in a few weeks because there is no lender underwriting or appraisal to wait on. Title work, lien payoffs and recording still take their normal time.

faqs.q: How long does it take to sell a house in Scranton for cash?
faqs.a: A cash sale can close in a few weeks, since there is no lender underwriting or appraisal to wait on. The remaining steps are title work, payoff of any liens and recording the deed with the Lackawanna County Recorder of Deeds.

faqs.q: Who pays the transfer tax on a Scranton home sale?
faqs.a: The sales agreement decides, and in most deals the seller and buyer split it. The state and local governments only care that the 3.7 percent total is paid when the deed is recorded.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Scranton rental property without a rental license?
faqs.a: You can sell it, but an unlicensed rental is a violation, and the city can refuse a license or fine the owner. Apply for or renew the license first if tenants are in the unit, since renewals are due March 15.

faqs.q: Does Scranton require an inspection before I can sell?
faqs.a: Permit work is inspected, and rentals follow a three-year inspection cycle. Ask the Code Enforcement office whether anything is open on your address before you list.

faqs.q: Is mine subsidence insurance required when buying a Scranton home?
faqs.a: The state does not require it, but a lender may ask for it when the property sits over mined ground. DEP sells the coverage, and the new owner has to apply for a new policy because the seller's does not transfer.
